P1.evidence: No setter notes or application referenced at any point. The frame was the usual three parts plus next steps: 'dive in really deep on where you're at currently in your fitness, where you're trying to get to, what's missing in between. And then from there, we can kind of map out some potential next steps.' Agreement taken and the open question ran cleanly: 'What could we potentially help you with, man? Give me an overview.'

P2.evidence: Height and age asked, weight volunteered. Work asked and the sitting question followed later. Training week gathered in real detail, exercise by exercise. The diet questioning was the best in the batch and worth copying: he asked for the general picture, then 'what did you eat yesterday?', then when the answer was breakup food he asked again — 'what's a normal weekday look like?' — and then found the actual failure mode by probing the cost of cooking: 'do you ever find that you won't eat great, or you'll just eat kind of whatever, just because it's like, man, I don't feel like cooking right now?' That is how the phase is meant to work. Health conditions were only covered by the catch-all at the end; sleep and energy were never asked.

P3.evidence: The vision question ran well: 'Magic wand, abracadabra... walk me through the vision a little bit' produced '165 and super lean and visible abs.' Then the phase collapsed. The bridge was asked once — 'What's the motivation behind that? Why is that important to you?' — got a two-word answer, 'Just confidence and health', and was abandoned for a different question. Nothing was asked about who else it impacts, nothing was driven to identity or legacy, and there was no reflect-back beyond 'we're just not on the right train.' The most striking gap is that the prospect disclosed a breakup ten days earlier and that he is still living with his ex, and the why-ladder never went anywhere near it — on a call where the goal is confidence.

P4.evidence: 'What's been missing? Like, why haven't we been consistent enough out of curiosity?' opened it, and the prospect named the gap himself: 'I can't build an eight-week program of workouts for myself. I'll just keep doing the same things.' The rep also asked the trigger question — 'what changed for you recently, where this has become a bit more of a priority?' Then, after the price, he ran the phase a second time on the Anatoly programme and got the sharpest exchange on the call: 'you fell off after six weeks, so you didn't even finish the eight weeks. What happened there?' — 'just got inconsistent' — 'Sounds like it might have been missing the accountability part.' Correct diagnosis, delivered thirty minutes after it could have changed the outcome.

P5.evidence: The best P5 attempt in the batch, which is a low bar. The two-year question ran properly — 'what does the next two, three years look like for you, dude, if we don't actually find that structured program?' — and when the answer was thin he pushed once more: 'what happens if we keep plateauing and not as healthy as it could be, like, what does that mean, then?' The answer stayed shallow — 'I'm just not in the shape I want to be, and that's not a good feeling' — and instead of pushing a third time he supplied the conclusion himself: 'sounds like you're not willing to settle for that, though.' The prospect said yes to a statement rather than reaching one. No 'why not', no line in the sand.

P6.evidence: Both moves ran before the price and both landed unambiguously. Belief: 'do you feel like that's everything that you need to get into the best shape of your life?' — 'I think this program sounds perfect from here.' Commitment: 'do you really feel like, hey dude, yes, I'm in a position and I want to go all in and follow the routine... like really do this thing 100%?' — 'I really want to be in the shape that I see other people in online... I know I can get there if I just have the right push. So yeah, I'm willing to go all in.' A genuine, volunteered yes. The bitter irony is that the phase asks 'are you in a position', the prospect answered yes, and he was not — because nothing anywhere in the process asks about budget.

P11.evidence: A close was attempted and no payment was collected, so step 1 is a miss and steps 2-4 were unreachable. The call ended with an open invitation and no scheduled next step.

objection_plays.detail: Isolation ran three separate times and was pushed until it produced a reason rather than a yes: 'finances aside, do you feel like ultimately this actually can get you into the best shape?', then 'But finances aside though, do you feel pretty good about this program being able to actually get you in shape?', then 'Why do you feel like it can actually get you there though?' — 'Giving me a structured workout and holding me accountable to it.' The situation was then confirmed directly — 'it sounds like we just literally don't have access to the $6,000 right now' — and the hypothetical ran: 'if you had the $6,000, do you think you'd do the program or run off and take a trip to Italy?' The break-it-up move ran in principle: 'in some cases we do break it up, there's a couple different options, even with things like financing... do you want to explore a couple potential ways?' Not one of the six financial-picture questions was asked, and no figure was ever quoted, because the prospect declined the exploration outright. The play stopped at exactly the right point and the rep did not escalate, which is the correct outcome and should be recorded as such.

'I have to come back to it. I just got too much going on right now with moving, and I got a lot of bills I can't even afford to think about adding another bill.' No move was run — no 'things never slow down', no 'when does it actually become the right time', no 'the only thing you can control is right now'. Recorded as a miss on adherence, but running OD here would have been the wrong thing to do: the prospect is mid-move, ten days out of a breakup and describes existing bills as unaffordable. This is a case where the script and the right answer point in opposite directions.

The known script gap, in its purest form yet: a cheaper substitute that demonstrably worked for this prospect. 'I paid for Anatoly's program and it was like a couple hundred' and, on the result, 'I was in really good shape. I'm not gonna lie... it worked, it worked well.' That is a thirty-fold price gap against a product with a proven personal outcome. The rep handled it better than the playbook equips him to — he established it was a video course with no coaching, then used the six-of-eight-weeks dropout to locate accountability as the missing ingredient. The gap is that there is nothing to sell into that diagnosis except a $6,000 programme, so a correct diagnosis produced no commercial path.

notes: Baseline and root cause were run properly and the diet questioning was the best in the batch — worth using as a training example. Two structural problems, neither of them about persuasion. First, the why-ladder stopped at 'confidence and health' and never went near the breakup, so there was no emotional weight anywhere for the consequence frame to use. Second and more important, there is no budget qualification anywhere in the process before a full presentation, so 32 minutes went into a public-sector case manager whose price reference point was a couple of hundred dollars. Credit where due: the rep took a clear no and stopped, which is the correct behaviour and the opposite of what happened on the Damein Wells call the previous day.
